subject: physics
title: Atoms and isotopes

concepts.def: The smallest particle of an element that still behaves as that element. Atoms are very small, having a radius of about 1 x 10^-10 metres.

The tiny positively charged centre of an atom, composed of both protons and neutrons. Its radius is less than 1/10 000 of the radius of the atom, yet most of the mass of the atom is concentrated in it.
A positively charged particle found in the nucleus. Every nucleus of a given element contains the same number of protons.
An uncharged particle found in the nucleus alongside the protons. Changing the number of neutrons gives a different isotope of the same element.
A negatively charged particle arranged at different distances from the nucleus, outside it. In an atom the number of electrons equals the number of protons.
The nucleus is less than one ten-thousandth of the atomic radius, so on a scale drawing of an atom the nucleus would be invisible and the atom is mostly empty space.
One of the different distances from the nucleus at which electrons in an atom are arranged. Electrons further from the nucleus are at higher energy levels.
When an atom absorbs electromagnetic radiation an electron may move further from the nucleus, to a higher energy level.
When an electron moves closer to the nucleus, to a lower energy level, the atom emits electromagnetic radiation.
An atom has no overall electrical charge because the number of negative electrons equals the number of positive protons in the nucleus.
The number of protons in an atom of an element. All atoms of a particular element have the same atomic number.
The total number of protons and neutrons in an atom.
The conventional representation of an atom, with the mass number written above the atomic number to the left of the chemical symbol, for example mass number 23 and atomic number 11 for sodium.
One of two or more atoms of the same element that have the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons, and therefore different mass numbers.
An atom that has lost one or more outer electrons, so that protons outnumber electrons and the particle carries a positive charge.
A description or picture used to explain observations. New experimental evidence may lead to a scientific model being changed or replaced.
The idea, held before the discovery of the electron, that atoms were tiny spheres that could not be divided.
The model that followed the discovery of the electron: the atom is a ball of positive charge with negative electrons embedded in it.
The experiment whose results led to the conclusion that the mass of an atom was concentrated at the centre and that the nucleus was charged.
The model in which the mass and the charge of an atom are concentrated in a tiny central nucleus, with electrons outside it. It replaced the plum pudding model.
Niels Bohr's adaptation of the nuclear model, in which electrons orbit the nucleus at specific distances. His theoretical calculations agreed with experimental observations.

Later experiments led to the idea that the positive charge of any nucleus could be subdivided into a whole number of smaller particles, each with the same amount of positive charge; these were named protons.
The experimental work of James Chadwick provided the evidence for neutrons within the nucleus, about 20 years after the nucleus became an accepted scientific idea.

mcqs.q: Which of these is closest to the radius of a typical atom?
options: About 1 x 10^-10 m, a ten-billionth of a metre
About 1 x 10^-15 m, the size of a nucleus
About 1 x 10^-6 m, a thousandth of a mm
About 1 x 10^-3 m, the width of a pin head
mcqs.explain: The specification gives the radius of an atom as about 1 x 10^-10 metres.

mcqs.q: Which statement describes the basic structure of an atom?
options: A positive nucleus of protons and electrons, with neutrons outside
A positive nucleus of protons and neutrons, surrounded by electrons
A negative nucleus of protons and neutrons, with electrons outside it
A core of neutrons only, with protons and electrons around it
mcqs.explain: This is the structure given in the specification: a positively charged nucleus composed of protons and neutrons, surrounded by negatively charged electrons.

mcqs.q: How does the radius of a nucleus compare with the radius of the atom?
options: It is about 1/10 of the atom's radius, as pictured
It is roughly 1/100 of the atom's radius in all atoms
It is less than 1/10 000 of the atom's radius
It is about half of the atom's whole radius
mcqs.explain: The specification states that the radius of a nucleus is less than 1/10 000 of the radius of an atom.

mcqs.q: Where is nearly all of the mass of an atom found?
options: In the electrons, because there are so many of them
Spread out evenly throughout the atom's volume
In the nucleus, which holds the protons only
In the nucleus, in the protons and neutrons
mcqs.explain: Most of the mass of an atom is concentrated in the nucleus.

mcqs.q: An electron in an atom absorbs electromagnetic radiation. What happens to that electron?
options: It moves closer to the nucleus, to a lower energy level
It moves further from the nucleus, to a higher energy level
It escapes the atom, leaving behind a positive ion
It stays where it is but orbits a little quicker
mcqs.explain: Absorption of electromagnetic radiation moves an electron further from the nucleus, to a higher energy level.

mcqs.q: An atom emits electromagnetic radiation. What has one of its electrons done?
options: Moved further from the nucleus, to a higher energy level
Left the atom, carrying the energy away with it
Moved closer to the nucleus, to a lower energy level
Settled at a new distance of its own choosing
mcqs.explain: Emission of electromagnetic radiation accompanies an electron moving closer to the nucleus, to a lower energy level.

mcqs.q: Why does an atom have no overall electrical charge?
options: Its neutrons cancel out the charge of the protons
It has just as many electrons as it has neutrons
Its charges are much too small to be noticed
It has equal numbers of protons and electrons
mcqs.explain: In an atom the number of electrons is equal to the number of protons, so the charges cancel.

mcqs.q: What is the atomic number of an element?
options: The number of protons in the nucleus
The number of protons and neutrons added
The number of electrons in the outer shell
The number of neutrons in the nucleus
mcqs.explain: The number of protons in an atom of an element is called its atomic number.

mcqs.q: What does the mass number of an atom tell you?
options: The number of neutrons in the nucleus of the atom
The number of protons and electrons in the atom
The total number of protons and neutrons in the atom
The mass of a single atom, measured in grams
mcqs.explain: The total number of protons and neutrons in an atom is called its mass number.

mcqs.q: An atom of sodium has mass number 23 and atomic number 11. How many neutrons are in its nucleus?
options: 11 neutrons, since 11 is the smaller number
34 neutrons, found from 23 + 11 = 34
23 neutrons, the larger of the numbers
12 neutrons, worked out from 23 - 11 = 12
mcqs.explain: Mass number = protons + neutrons, so neutrons = 23 - 11 = 12.

mcqs.q: In the conventional representation of an atom, what does the lower number stand for?
options: The atomic number, which counts the protons
The mass number, the protons plus the neutrons
The number of neutrons found inside the nucleus
The charge held by the nucleus in coulombs
mcqs.explain: The lower number is the atomic number: the number of protons in the atom.

mcqs.q: What are isotopes of an element?
options: Atoms which have different numbers of protons
Atoms with equal protons, unequal neutrons
Atoms of the element that have lost an electron
Atoms of two different elements with the same mass
mcqs.explain: Atoms of the same element can have different numbers of neutrons; these atoms are called isotopes of that element.

mcqs.q: How does an atom turn into a positive ion?
options: By gaining one or more electrons from elsewhere
By gaining one extra proton into its nucleus
By losing one neutron from its own nucleus
By losing one or more electrons from its outer shell
mcqs.explain: Atoms turn into positive ions if they lose one or more outer electrons.

mcqs.q: Chlorine-35 and chlorine-37 are isotopes. Which statement about them is correct?
options: They have the same atomic number but different mass numbers
They have different atomic numbers and different mass numbers
They have the same mass number but a different charge
They have different numbers of electrons in an atom
mcqs.explain: Isotopes of an element share the proton number and therefore the atomic number, but differ in neutrons and so in mass number.

mcqs.q: A lithium atom with mass number 7 and atomic number 3 loses one electron. What is the resulting ion?
options: Charge -1, because one electron has been removed
Charge +1, mass number is still 7, 3 protons
Charge +1, mass number 6, with 3 protons still
Charge +1, mass number 8, a proton joined
mcqs.explain: Losing one electron leaves one more proton than electron, so the charge is +1. The nucleus is untouched, so mass number 7 and 3 protons remain.

mcqs.q: What should happen to an accepted scientific model when new experimental evidence does not fit it?
options: The model is kept, since it is proved
The evidence is put down to an error
The model is changed or is replaced
The model is kept and the result ignored
mcqs.explain: New experimental evidence may lead to a scientific model being changed or replaced.

mcqs.q: How were atoms described before the discovery of the electron?
options: As tiny spheres that could not be divided at all
As tiny spheres with a nucleus at their centre
As balls of positive charge full of electrons
As clouds of charge with no definite shape
mcqs.explain: Before the discovery of the electron, atoms were thought to be tiny spheres that could not be divided.

mcqs.q: What did the plum pudding model suggest about the atom?
options: The atom has a small positive nucleus with electrons orbiting
The atom is a ball of positive charge with electrons in it
The atom is a ball of negative charge with protons in it
The atom is a solid sphere that cannot be split at all
mcqs.explain: The plum pudding model suggested that the atom is a ball of positive charge with negative electrons embedded in it.

mcqs.q: In the alpha particle scattering experiment, what happened to most of the alpha particles?
options: They bounced straight back from the metal foil
They were deflected by exactly the same angle
They passed straight through the metal foil
They were absorbed and stopped in the foil
mcqs.explain: Most alpha particles passed straight through, which showed that the atom is mostly empty space.

mcqs.q: What is the key difference between the plum pudding model and the nuclear model?
options: The nuclear model has the electrons embedded in charge
The plum pudding model has a nucleus at its centre
The plum pudding model gave the atom a net charge
The nuclear model puts the charge at the centre
mcqs.explain: In the nuclear model the mass of an atom is concentrated at the centre and that nucleus is charged, rather than the charge being spread through the whole atom.

mcqs.q: What did Niels Bohr add to the nuclear model of the atom?
options: Electrons may orbit the nucleus at any distance
Electrons orbit the nucleus at specific distances only
The nucleus lies at the centre and holds the mass
The nucleus contains neutrons as well as protons
mcqs.explain: Bohr adapted the nuclear model by suggesting that electrons orbit the nucleus at specific distances, and his calculations agreed with observations.

mcqs.q: Later experiments showed that the positive charge of any nucleus could be subdivided. What followed from this?
options: The nuclear charge was shown to be a single indivisible lump
The neutron was named, a particle carrying no charge
The proton was named, each carrying equal positive charge
The nucleus itself was shown to be negatively charged
mcqs.explain: The charge was found to be a whole number of equal smaller particles, and the name proton was given to these particles.

mcqs.q: What did the experimental work of James Chadwick provide evidence for?
options: The existence of a nucleus in every atom
The existence of protons inside all atomic nuclei
The existence of electron energy levels in atoms
The existence of neutrons within the nucleus
mcqs.explain: Chadwick's experimental work provided the evidence to show the existence of neutrons within the nucleus.

mcqs.q: Why did the scattering experiment lead scientists to change the model of the atom?
options: A few alpha particles bounced back, which the old model forbade
Scientists preferred the newer picture because it was simpler to draw
Every alpha particle bounced back, showing the atom is solid all through
The experiment showed that electrons must sit in fixed energy levels
mcqs.explain: A ball of evenly spread positive charge could not repel a fast alpha particle backwards, so the evidence forced a new model with a tiny, dense, charged nucleus.
